text: technical insights into developing the commercial reactor and process for plastic waste conversion. The major findings are highlighted below: 1. Compared to pyrolysis temperature, vapor residence time in the continuous pyrolysis reactor exhibited a greater impact on the product distribution and composition. Extended residence time strongly promoted lighter oils. 2. The post-consumer waste plastics produced overall lower yields of condensables and higher yields of gases and char than virgin plastics. The variations were primarily due to additives, fillers and pigments embedded in plastics. Prewashing plastics cannot remove these impurities. 3. This work successfully demonstrated the continuous production of condensable products (oil and wax) from unwashed post-consumer wastes. This was achieved at the laboratory scale (~500 g/h) under pyrolysis and TOD conditions, and at the pilot- scale (~2.5 kg/h) under TOD conditions. Operation under TOD conditions demonstrated dramatic reductions in energy demand of up to 80% compared to pyrolysis conditions and approached autothermal operation. This can have a significant impact on energy requirements for commercial processes and further reduces the heat transfer limitations in large reactors. Iowa State University’s fluidized- bed reactor design with low vapor residence times (~1 second) demonstrated high condensable yields (>80 wt.%), which preserves carbon for further catalytic upgrading. 4. TOD can lower the energy consumption of waste plastic pyrolysis without significantly reducing the condensable yield. However, TOD products also include a small fraction of aqueous oils enriched in oxygenated compounds. 5. This project delivered a quantitatively validated diagnosis of current model limitations, generated first-principles kinetic and thermodynamic data to address them, and demonstrated scalability from small to larger hydrocarbon surrogates. The results strengthen the mechanistic foundation required for predictive plastic pyrolysis modeling and rational process design. Topic Area 4 – Catalytic Upgrading of Plastic Oils into Aromatics and Olefins: By systematically varying acid site composition through metal incorporation via solid-state methods, the team established clear structure-function relationships controlling product selectivity for catalytic conversion of pyrolysis oils. The M2 catalyst with metal-modified acid sites achieved markedly enhanced olefin production compared to conventional aluminum-only catalysts, validating hypotheses based on transition state stabilization theory. This accomplishment is significant because it provides a rational design framework for tailoring product distributions to market needs without extensive trial-and- error optimization. The fundamental understanding gained enables targeted catalyst development for specific applications, whether maximizing olefins for polymerization, aromatics for chemical intermediates, or balanced distributions for fuel applications. The characterization suite developed during this work, particularly CD CN FT-IR for acid site speciation, provides powerful tools for future catalyst development efforts. ₃ Development of the optimized regeneration protocol (700°C, 6 hours, 20% O at 75 mL/min total flow) represents a critical breakthrough for practical implementation. Achieving >95% activity recovery per cycle while processing real-world PC₂ W-PP pyrolysis oil demonstrates commercial viability. The systematic optimization approach, evaluating temperature, oxygen concentration, flow rate, and duration, provides a methodology applicable to other catalyst systems and feedstocks. The significance of this achievement extends beyond immediate technical performance.
